subject: technology
essential_question: How can understanding how computers work help us explain, decide, create, or solve something that matters?
project_brief: Write a simple troubleshooting flowchart for a common device problem. This is the grade 4 culminating project for "How Computers Work" (ma-g4-tech-cs-u02, unit 2), built around hardware and software review, input process output, storage and memory basics, common problems and fixes, and safe basic troubleshooting steps. Work from a supplied, intentionally broken example related to hardware and software review, input process output, storage and memory basics, and common problems and fixes. Reproduce the failure, isolate the smallest case that triggers it, fix the underlying cause (not just the symptom), and keep a short defect log documenting what was wrong and how you know it is fixed now.
requirements: Address every topic listed for this unit: hardware and software review, input process output, storage and memory basics, common problems and fixes, safe basic troubleshooting steps, and keeping devices organized.
Meet the performance task as written: Write a simple troubleshooting flowchart for a common device problem.
Show your work or process, not just a final result — a process note, sketch log, commit history, or draft trail.
Complete the checklist in this package before submitting.
primary_task: Work from a supplied, intentionally broken example related to hardware and software review, input process output, storage and memory basics, and common problems and fixes. Reproduce the failure, isolate the smallest case that triggers it, fix the underlying cause (not just the symptom), and keep a short defect log documenting what was wrong and how you know it is fixed now.
test_or_check_criteria: Every claim or design choice in the submission can be traced to hardware and software review or another named topic from this unit — nothing is left unexplained.
The submission runs, displays, or demonstrates correctly on at least two different sample inputs or scenarios the student chooses.
No real password, API key, account credential, precise location, or other real personal/system data appears anywhere in the submission — fictional or sandbox examples only.
The student can explain, in their own words, why each step or decision was made, not just that it works.
A defect log lists each bug found, its symptom, its root cause, and the specific change that fixed it.
At least one test existed (or was written) that failed before the fix and passes after it, proving the fix actually worked.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: This project never touches a real account, a real password or API key, a live production system, or another person's real data. Use fictional names, sandbox environments, local files, or already-approved sample data throughout. Submit code, screenshots of your own sandbox, diagrams, or a written walkthrough — a live public deployment is never required.

copyright_and_authorship: The final submitted work must remain your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI assistant may help you plan, explain a concept, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but may not produce the graded work itself. Never request, store, or submit a real password, API key, access token, or other real credential; use only fictional accounts and sandboxed or offline systems.
remediation: If the project stalls, step back to the smallest version of the task: rebuild just the part covering hardware and software review in isolation, using a worked example from this unit as a model, then re-attach it to the full project once that smaller piece works and you can explain why.
extension: Once the core project is working, extend it to handle a new constraint or edge case related to input process output, or compare two different approaches to the same problem and explain the real tradeoff between them in your own words.
